title: Red Fe Lks Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Red Fe Lks wells have a 266-foot median depth, 4.0 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $23,300-$38,600.
h1: Red Fe Lks, Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
For rural property near Red Fe Lks in Larimer County, the well record points to fractured mountain bedrock rather than a predictable shallow groundwater setting. Permitted wells within 5 miles show a wide range of depths and production. Most are domestic or household wells, and the named aquifer records are primarily unnamed fractured bedrock.

The numbers can help screen a property, but they do not replace a site-specific well bid, permit review, water-quality testing, or a careful look at nearby wells. Red Feather Lakes is the closest named area in the records, with Livermore, Bellvue, Glen Haven, Laporte, and Drake providing broader local context.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Red Fe Lks?
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Red Fe Lks is 266 feet. The middle half runs from 140 to 440 feet, so a drilling proposal near the median is not unusual, but a property at either end of that range needs a different budget conversation. The 90th percentile is 600 feet, and the deepest well in the record reaches 901 feet.

Depths reflect fractured mountain bedrock, identified on most permits as unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifer. Granite, gneiss, and related fractured rock can produce water through specific fractures rather than through a uniform underground layer. That is why nearby wells can differ substantially. A driller should review neighboring completions, access, casing and grout requirements, and the expected target depth before giving a firm price.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Red Fe Lks well make?
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 4.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 6.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells fall in the 1-to-5-gallon-per-minute range, while 39% report 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Only 3% report more than 15 gallons per minute, and 7% report under 1 gallon per minute.

For a buyer, the median is a planning point, not a guarantee. A 4.0-gallon-per-minute well can serve a typical household when storage and the pressure system are designed correctly, but low production may require a larger tank and careful peak-use planning. Ask for the pumping test, recovery information, well construction report, and permit conditions. A domestic exempt well is subject to Colorado’s 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: What does the water table show near Red Fe Lks?
sections.html:
Among the 111 wells reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 100 feet, with the middle half from 34 to 100 feet below the ground surface. That is useful for estimating pump setting and trench planning, but the measurement is not the same as a guaranteed pumping level. Water levels can change with season, recharge, pumping, and local geology.

The decade figures show a deeper reported median in the 2010s and 2020s than in the 1980s: 25 feet below surface in the 1980s, compared with 100 feet in both the 2010s and 2020s. This suggests lower measured water levels in the later records, but the small reporting set and changing well locations make it poor evidence of a uniform regional decline. Have a driller evaluate the specific parcel.

sections.heading: Who has drilled wells near Red Fe Lks?
sections.html:
The permit history is long, with records beginning in the 1950s and the newest permit year being 2025. The largest period of activity appears in the 1970s through the 2000s, while permits continue in the 2010s and 2020s. Of 1,783 wells in the Colorado DWR records, 1,342 are recorded as constructed, 1,390 report total depth, and 812 report pump yield.

The most active drillers named in these records are Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.), Hersh & Son Well Drilling Inc. (Hersh, Harry), and Lesh Drilling Inc. (Lesh Jr., Ed). These records identify historical permit activity, not a recommendation or a promise of current availability. Before hiring, verify licensing, insurance, references, scheduling, access requirements, and exactly what the bid includes.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost in Red Fe Lks?
sections.html:
In fractured mountain bedrock, a planning rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 266 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at $17,300 to $26,600. A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $23,300 to $38,600.

Those figures are budgeting ranges, not a guaranteed contract price. The final number can move with access, casing and grout, drilling conditions, water production, pump depth, trench length, electrical work, and whether the hole must be deepened. Get the driller to separate footage, casing, testing, pump equipment, storage, trenching, and electrical in writing. A low bid that excludes site work may not be the lower completed cost.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building or buying
sections.html:
Low yield and dry-hole risk deserve special attention in fractured granite and gneiss. The records include 7% of reported yields under 1 gallon per minute, and reported depths range to 901 feet. Ask what happens if drilling reaches the contract limit without an adequate supply, and confirm the property’s water right or exempt-well status with Colorado DWR.

Water quality also needs independent testing. Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 12 historic mine features, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those map results do not determine a parcel’s water quality. Test the well for relevant contaminants, especially if the property is near a mine feature or a PFAS site. Confirm septic setbacks, soil suitability, driveway access, building envelope, and space for a replacement septic system before closing.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Red Fe Lks lot
sections.html:
Start with the neighboring-well review. Compare depths, reported yields, static levels, aquifer descriptions, construction details, and permit uses around the parcel, including records associated with Red Feather Lakes and the other nearby areas. Treat the comparison as a range, not as a guarantee: fractured-bedrock wells can change quickly over short distances.

For a purchase, make the contract contingent on reviewing the well permit, construction report, pump test, water-quality results, and legal water use. For a new build, have the driller and septic designer coordinate the well location, access route, electrical trench, storage equipment, and septic reserve area before excavation. Budget around the local cost range, then carry room for deeper drilling or site complications. That approach is more reliable than using a single nearby well as the estimate.

faq.a: The median reported depth is 266 feet. The middle half of wells falls between 140 and 440 feet, while the 90th percentile is 600 feet. The deepest well in the record is 901 feet. Because most permits identify fractured bedrock, nearby wells can vary considerably, so a local driller should review surrounding completions before pricing a new well.

faq.q: What is the typical well yield in Red Fe Lks?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 4.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 3.0 to 6.0 gallons per minute. About 7% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute, while 39% are 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Ask for the pumping test and plan storage carefully if production is near the low end.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Red Fe Lks?
faq.a: The estimated drilling rate in fractured mountain bedrock is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 266-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $17,300 to $26,600. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $23,300 to $38,600. Access and deeper drilling can change the final bid.

faq.a: The permit map shows 2 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 12 historic mine features within about 10 miles, with 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those facts do not establish the quality of a particular well. Test before purchase or occupancy, and choose testing based on nearby mine features, PFAS information, septic conditions, and the well’s construction.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Red Fe Lks?
faq.a: Reported median static water levels were 25 feet below surface in the 1980s and 100 feet in both the 2010s and 2020s. That is a deeper later measurement, but only 111 wells report static water levels, and the records cover different locations and conditions. The series suggests a change in reported levels, not proof of a uniform regional decline.
